title: The End Is Drawing Near
mood: The night before, Vexana keeps watch from a ruined tower over one lit window.

hero.alt: A small gold star badge glows in a wash of pale light.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 28

segs.t: Vexana woke curled beside the folded uniform. Over her the four Guards stood dark, as they always did after she slept.
She bared her right wrist. The star was lit.
On the far side of the body, the Storm Citadel was moving.
She sat up. Since it came, it had hung at the body’s side in its violet storm. Now it slid away, slow. In the flashes of its lightning, the black blades showed.
As it went, its storm drew in tight around the blades. It crossed the dark to the crack and stopped just behind its mouth. There it hung, and did not move again.
The crack was nearly whole. Days ago she had stopped measuring it with her thumb. Now her whole hand at arm’s length would not cover it. Through it lay a gray sky over the bay, going dim with dusk.
Cloud began to pour through the crack into that sky. It spread out over the water, and lightning flickered in it.
Her storm,
Vexana thought.
It goes on ahead of her.
Then the body moved. In all her weeks in the dark its great bulk had never once changed its place. Now its edge slid a long way toward the crack, slowly, and was still again.
On the prow she had not asked Obsidia when. The crack would tell her, she had thought. Now it had.
Tomorrow.
“The end is drawing near,” said Vexana.
Nothing in the hollow answered.
She stood and laid her palm on the lead Guard’s chest, over the heart. Under her glove a hum began. The yellow eyes lit, and the heart blazed magenta. High in the dark, the giants’ eyes lit after it.
She looked up at it a long time. She knew each of its plates by the dents her hammer had left.
“Until tomorrow,” she told it.
She let them go dark, the giants first. The heart went out last. When the body came she would need all her power. Tonight none of it could go to them.
The pink-haired keychain lay on the folded uniform, its little face turned up to her.
Every night since the park, it had gone into the white box on her desk, with her star beside it. That had been the last thing she did each day.
She picked it up and clipped it inside her sleeve, against her wrist, beside the star. It lay cool on her skin. The star was warm next to it.
“Now you have me on yours,” Guinevere had said, pressing it into her palm at the stall.

Vexana pulled the sleeve down over both of them. The uniform she left where it lay, folded square, as she had laid it in the first weeks. In the vision she had worn it, and Guinevere had fallen anyway.
The cold point under her breastbone stirred.
“The dome’s edge. Tonight.”
No feeders came out of the dark to go with her. Tonight it wanted only her eyes. In front of her the dark opened, and she stepped through.
Beyond the dome. That night.
The door let her out on the rise below the ruined tower. Off the dead ground the wind blew dry. The rain had not reached it yet.

The stair inside the tower had no rail and half its steps. She climbed it with one hand on the wall, the way she had climbed the wall stair at home behind her father. At the top he had always pointed out over the dead ground and told her to look.
She looked. Tonight there were no stars over it. Cloud had come in from the bay and covered them all. Not even the small one he had given her.
She turned to the city.

Thunderheads stood over the dome. Lightning ran through them out over the bay, and rain blew across the water. Inside the shell the city was lit, street after street. The Academy’s beam climbed into the cloud.
On Joe’s last slide, every machine under that ship’s storm had died. Here the lamps still burned.
Its weather,
she thought.
The ship itself is still behind the sky.
Over the bay, between two thunderheads, a small pale point showed. From the void she could not cover it with her hand. From here a fingernail would have hidden it.
Every window in the girls’ wing was dark. High on the Academy’s tower, one window was lit: the lab’s glass room.
Still up there,
she thought.
Still looking.
The hour of the call came and went. Her hand stayed on her staff.
On the late nights, Guinevere had bargained.
“Ten more.”
“Go to bed.”
“Five. You can count them.”
Vexana had counted every one, down the line. She still knew the phone number by heart. Gold ink, underlined twice.
For emergencies. Or anything.
Tonight is both,
she thought.
Her room would be as she had left it. The photo in its thin black frame, the two of them hand in hand. The felt dolls beside it, finished, the card under them.
For Guinevere. Same place, next year.
Her father’s screwdriver, wiped clean, in its place in the toolbox. The white box, and no keychain in it.
Someone would have to clear that room.
Let it be her,
Vexana thought.
Let her read the card. Then go next year anyway, Guinevere. Don’t go alone.
The rain reached the dead ground. It swept across the broken streets below and hissed on the stone around her boots.
She looked down at her staff. She tried the brass collar with her fingers, the way her father had tried each sight on the wall. It did not give.

Out on the bay the water lay black under the rain. Tomorrow the body would hang over it, whole, and open its chest to fire. By then she would be in front of it, with the Guard’s heart shut around her. When the chest opened, she would let her power go into it, all of it, at once.
She had known since she knelt before the Will what that would cost. She had not changed her mind once.
It thinks I am its eyes on a tower,
she thought.
All these weeks, and it has never looked twice at my sleeve.
“If night is fated to swallow day, I will vanish before the dawn,” Vexana told the rain.
The Guards will still be standing after,
she thought.
Over her.
The night went on, and the lab’s light did not go out.
Long past midnight she found she was humming. It was her father’s march, the one from the gun pit. She stopped where he always stopped.
“I’ll finish it when the war does,” he had said.
Tomorrow, maybe,
she thought.
And nobody knows the rest.
She turned her wrist up under the sleeve. Through the cloth she could feel them both, the star’s warmth and the doll’s small head beside it.
Go to bed,
she nearly said.
It means goodnight,
she thought.
It promises another night.
She did not say it.
“I will become the sun that lights the dark night, and protect her,” she told the window.
Lightning lit the bay white. For a moment the whole Academy stood out against the cloud, its tower black, the one window small and gold at the top. Then the dark came back around it.
Before first light the door opened behind her, as it always did.
The night had been hers. She had spent all of it here.
She turned to the door. At its edge she looked back over her shoulder.
Across the city the window still burned. Rain swept between them, and the light blurred and went gray. Then it was there again. Out over the bay, lightning.
The door shut on the sight of that window, still lit.
